rounds.t: Brain lesion localization and abnormal posturing

q.s: A 58-year-old man becomes impulsive, makes inappropriate jokes, overeats and shows no empathy for his family. Memory is relatively preserved. Which region is most affected?
e: Correct. Frontal lobe syndrome, as in frontotemporal dementia.

q.s: A patient with a right MCA stroke and left hemiplegia has eyes deviated to the right. Which structure is damaged?
e: Correct. Eyes look toward the lesion, away from the hemiplegia.
Wrong. Eyes look away from the lesion.

q.s: A right-handed man has agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation after a stroke. Which region is affected?
After a right parietal stroke, a woman ignores the left side of her body and only eats food on the right side of her plate. Diagnosis?
A 70-year-old man with hypertension suddenly develops wild flinging movements of his right arm and leg. Where is the lesion?
A man with chronic alcohol use is confused, ataxic and has eye movement abnormalities. Later he has profound memory loss and confabulates. Which structures are damaged bilaterally?
e: Correct. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency.

q.s: After HSV-1 encephalitis, a man becomes hypersexual, puts objects in his mouth and overeats. Which structure is damaged bilaterally?
Bilateral hippocampal damage causes:
e: Correct. Inability to form new memories, as in Alzheimer disease.

q.s: A boy with a pineal tumor cannot look upward and has pupils that constrict with accommodation but not light. Which region is compressed?
A 30-year-old woman with MS cannot adduct her left eye on right gaze, and her right eye shows nystagmus on abduction. Convergence is intact. Which structure is affected?
e: Wrong. Left eye fails to adduct.

q.s: A man with chronic alcohol use has a wide-based "drunken sailor" gait, nystagmus and dysarthria with normal finger-to-nose testing. Which region is degenerated?
A patient with a right cerebellar hemisphere lesion falls toward which side, and where is his intention tremor?
A comatose patient flexes the arms and extends the legs to a painful stimulus. Where is the lesion?
o: Between the red and vestibular nuclei
Above the red nucleus (often cerebral cortex)
e: Correct. Decorticate posturing ("hands near the cor").

q.s: Decerebrate posturing results from overactivity of which tract?
e: Correct. Upper and lower limb extension.

q.s: Which posturing has a worse prognosis?
A lesion of the paramedian pontine reticular formation causes the eyes to look:
o: Away from the lesion, toward the hemiplegia

q.s: Damage to the reticular activating system causes:
Which basal ganglia disorders cause resting tremor and chorea?
Decorticate posturing results from overactivity of which tracts?
The cerebellar hemispheres affect which body regions?
o: Lateral (distal) limbs on the same side

rounds.t: Ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, and cerebral edema

q.s: Irreversible neuronal injury begins after how many minutes of hypoxia?
Which brain regions are most vulnerable to hypoxia?
o: Hippocampus (CA1), neocortex, cerebellar Purkinje cells and watershed areas

q.s: Which imaging study must be done before giving tPA for stroke?
Which imaging study can detect ischemia within 3–30 minutes?
Brain tissue 12–24 hours after an infarct shows:
o: Red neurons with eosinophilic cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei

q.s: Brain tissue 3–5 days after an infarct shows predominantly:
Brain infarction results in which type of necrosis?
A patient with atrial fibrillation has infarcts in several vascular territories. Which stroke type is this?
A young woman with a stroke is found to have a DVT and a patent foramen ovale. Which mechanism caused her stroke?
tPA may be given for ischemic stroke within what time window?
o: 3–4.5 hours of onset, if no hemorrhage or bleeding risk

q.s: Which additional treatment is used for a large-artery occlusion?
A 65-year-old has sudden loss of vision in his right eye "like a curtain coming down" that resolves in 5 minutes. MRI is normal. Which source is most likely?
o: Emboli from right carotid artery disease
e: Correct. Amaurosis fugax, a type of TIA.

q.s: A TIA is defined as:
o: Focal deficit lasting >24 hours with infarct on MRI
Brief reversible focal dysfunction without acute infarction on MRI

q.s: Cytotoxic cerebral edema results from:
o: Intracellular fluid accumulation from Na+/K+-ATPase dysfunction

q.s: A patient with a metastatic brain tumor has a large area of surrounding edema. Which type is this?
e: Correct. BBB disruption from tumors, trauma, hemorrhage, late ischemia.

q.s: Thrombotic strokes most commonly involve which artery?
e: Correct. Usually over a ruptured plaque.

q.s: Brain tissue more than 2 weeks after infarction shows:
Hypoxic strokes during cardiovascular surgery tend to affect:
Which risk reduction measures are used after ischemic stroke?
o: Antiplatelets, control of BP, glucose and lipids, and smoking cessation

q.s: A noncontrast CT typically becomes positive for ischemic stroke after:
e: Wrong. Too early; DWI MRI is positive by then.

q.s: A 70-year-old woman has weakness and numbness of her right leg and urinary incontinence. Her arm and face are normal. Which artery is occluded?
A right-handed man has right face and arm weakness and cannot produce fluent speech. Which artery is occluded?
A hypertensive man suddenly develops pure weakness of his left face, arm and leg with no sensory loss, aphasia, neglect or visual loss. Which vessel is involved?
o: Lenticulostriate branch supplying the right internal capsule

q.s: Lacunar infarcts result from which vascular change?
o: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture in large arteries

q.s: A right-handed patient can write a sentence but cannot read it back. Visual fields show a right hemianopia with macular sparing. Which artery is occluded?
o: Left PCA with involvement of the splenium

q.s: A patient has a right CN III palsy and left hemiplegia. Which syndrome is this?
A man is awake and can blink and move his eyes vertically, but is quadriplegic and cannot speak. Which artery is occluded?
e: Correct. Locked-in syndrome; the reticular activating system is spared.

q.s: A patient has left facial paralysis including the forehead, decreased lacrimation and taste, vertigo, left hearing loss and loss of pain and temperature on the right body. Which artery is occluded?
e: Wrong. No facial nucleus or hearing involvement.

q.s: Hearing loss in an AICA stroke results from occlusion of which branch?

A 64-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing and hiccups. He has left ptosis and miosis, loss of pain and temperature on the left face and right body, and left limb ataxia. Which structure is specifically affected by this artery's occlusion?
e: Correct. Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from PICA occlusion.

q.s: A patient has left tongue deviation on protrusion, right arm and leg weakness, and loss of proprioception on the right. Which artery is occluded?
Which deficit is specific to PICA occlusion compared with AICA?
o: Contralateral body pain and temperature loss
Dysphagia and hoarseness from nucleus ambiguus involvement
e: Correct. "Don't pick a horse that can't eat."

q.s: A dominant-hemisphere MCA stroke involving the temporal lobe may cause which visual field defect along with Wernicke aphasia?
e: Correct. Meyer loop in the temporal lobe.

q.s: A nondominant MCA stroke typically causes:
A patient cannot recognize familiar faces after a stroke. Which territory is affected?
PCA occlusion causes contralateral hemianopia with:
In a basilar artery stroke, which eye movements are preserved?
Facial weakness in an AICA stroke differs from a cortical stroke because it:
o: Is an LMN lesion involving the forehead on the same side

q.s: The most common type of lacunar stroke is:
Ipsilateral Horner syndrome occurs in which stroke syndromes?
o: AICA and PICA (lateral pontine and lateral medullary)

rounds.t: Hemorrhage, birth injuries, post-stroke pain, and aphasia

q.s: A 26-week premature infant develops a bulging fontanelle, seizures and hypotension on day 2. Where does this bleeding originate?
o: Germinal matrix in the subventricular zone

q.s: After a prolonged labor, a newborn has soft scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and resolves in days. Diagnosis?
After vacuum delivery, a newborn has a firm swelling over the parietal bone that does not cross suture lines. Days later he is jaundiced. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Blood between skull and periosteum; indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

q.s: Hours after a vacuum delivery, a newborn has a diffuse, fluctuant scalp swelling extending to the neck, pallor and tachycardia. Which vessels were torn?
o: Emissary veins, bleeding between periosteum and galea
e: Correct. Subgaleal hemorrhage can cause shock.

q.s: A teenager hit in the side of the head with a baseball loses consciousness briefly, wakes and talks normally, then deteriorates an hour later with a dilated right pupil. CT shows a biconvex hyperdense collection that does not cross sutures. Which vessel ruptured?
e: Correct. Epidural hematoma with a lucid interval.

q.s: The thinnest area of the lateral skull, where fractures often tear the middle meningeal artery, is the:
An 80-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has worsening confusion over weeks after a minor fall. CT shows a hypodense crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Bridging veins; brain atrophy is a risk factor.

q.s: A woman suddenly develops "the worst headache of my life" and neck stiffness. CT is normal. Lumbar puncture shows xanthochromia. Which complication may occur 3–10 days later?
e: Correct. Subarachnoid hemorrhage; nimodipine may help.

q.s: Hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage most often occurs in the:
e: Correct. Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriate vessels.

q.s: An 82-year-old woman without hypertension has recurrent lobar hemorrhages. Which cause is most likely?
Months after a thalamic lacunar stroke, a patient has burning pain and allodynia on the opposite side of his body. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Central post-stroke pain from VPL lesions.

q.s: Phantom limb pain is associated with:
o: Reorganization of the primary somatosensory cortex

q.s: After a high-speed car crash, a man remains in a coma. CT is nearly normal, but MRI shows many punctate hemorrhages in white matter tracts. Diagnosis?
A patient speaks fluently but makes no sense ("word salad"), cannot follow commands and is unaware of the problem. Where is the lesion?
A patient has fluent speech and good comprehension but cannot repeat phrases. Which structure is damaged?
A patient with Broca aphasia typically:
o: Speaks nonfluently with intact comprehension and is frustrated

q.s: How does dysarthria differ from aphasia?
o: Dysarthria only occurs in the dominant hemisphere
Dysarthria is a language comprehension deficit
Dysarthria is a motor inability to produce speech; aphasia is a language deficit

q.s: Acute subdural hematomas are associated with:
o: High-energy trauma and appear hyperdense on CT
Arterial bleeding with a lucid interval

q.s: Neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage is more common in premature infants because of:
o: Reduced glial fiber support and impaired autoregulation of blood pressure

q.s: Global aphasia results from damage to:

rounds.t: Aneurysms, heat illness, seizures, and headaches

q.s: What is the most common site of a saccular (berry) aneurysm?
o: Junction of the ACom and ACA
e: Wrong. Common, but not most common.

q.s: Saccular aneurysms are associated with which genetic conditions?
A 50-year-old woman has a headache, a drooping left eyelid and a dilated left pupil with the eye turned down and out. Which aneurysm is most likely?
o: Left ICA aneurysm in the cavernous sinus

q.s: A growing ACom aneurysm may compress the optic chiasm, causing:
Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are associated with:
o: Chronic hypertension and intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the basal ganglia and thalamus

q.s: A marathon runner collapses on a hot day. Temperature is 41.5°C. He is confused, his urine is dark and creatinine is rising. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Rapid external cooling, rehydration and electrolyte correction
Acetaminophen to lower the set point

q.s: How does fever differ from heat stroke?
o: Fever results from cytokine activation; heat stroke from failure to dissipate heat

q.s: A patient has a seizure beginning with twitching of the right hand. She remains fully aware throughout. Which seizure type is this?
A 7-year-old girl has many brief episodes of staring with eyelid fluttering, without postictal confusion. Hyperventilation triggers an episode. Which EEG finding is expected?
Status epilepticus is defined as continuous seizure activity lasting at least:
o: 5 minutes, or recurrent seizures without return to baseline

q.s: What is the most common cause of new-onset seizures in a 75-year-old?
e: Correct. Also neurodegenerative disease, tumor, trauma.

q.s: Which features suggest a psychogenic nonepileptic event?
o: Prolonged episodes without postictal phase, with a normal video EEG

q.s: A woman has steady, bilateral bandlike headaches lasting several hours without nausea or aura. Which prophylactic drug may be used?
A 28-year-old woman has throbbing unilateral headaches lasting a day with nausea and light sensitivity, preceded by zigzag lines in her vision. Which neuropeptide is involved?
A 35-year-old man wakes nightly with excruciating pain around his right eye lasting 45 minutes, with tearing, nasal congestion and a droopy eyelid. What acute treatment is effective?
e: Correct. Cluster headache; prophylaxis with verapamil.

q.s: Which mnemonic describes migraine features?
o: POUND — Pulsatile, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling

q.s: A 60-year-old woman has seconds-long, electric shock–like pain in her right cheek triggered by chewing or touching her face. Most cases are caused by:
o: Compression of the CN V root by an aberrant vascular loop
e: Wrong. Not the most common cause.

q.s: First-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia is:
Which drug can be used for migraine prophylaxis?
o: Topiramate, propranolol, valproate or anti-CGRP antibodies

q.s: Which drug class is used for acute migraine attacks?
A patient on haloperidol feels an intense inner restlessness and cannot sit still. Diagnosis?
A man with cirrhosis has a flapping motion of his hands when he extends his wrists. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Hepatic encephalopathy, Wilson disease, metabolic disorders.

q.s: A 45-year-old has a tremor of both hands when holding a cup that improves after a glass of wine. His father had the same. What is first-line treatment?
A patient's finger oscillates more as it approaches a target. Which structure is damaged?
A writer develops sustained cramping of his hand when writing. What treatment is used?
A woman has unpleasant sensations in her legs at night with an urge to move them, relieved by walking. Which condition should be checked for?
e: Correct. Restless legs syndrome; also CKD and diabetes.

q.s: Chorea is seen in which conditions?
o: Huntington disease and acute rheumatic fever (Sydenham chorea)

q.s: A 68-year-old man has a resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity, slow movements and small handwriting. What inclusion is seen in his substantia nigra neurons?
A patient with parkinsonism has early falls, vertical gaze palsy and cognitive decline. MRI shows midbrain atrophy with a "hummingbird sign." Diagnosis?
e: Wrong. Not with vertical gaze palsy.

q.s: A 40-year-old man has chorea, depression and personality change. His father had similar symptoms beginning at age 50. What is the genetic defect?
o: CAG repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4

q.s: Huntington disease shows atrophy of which structures?
o: Caudate and putamen, with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly

q.s: Which neurotransmitter changes occur in Huntington disease?
Which is a reversible cause of dementia?
e: Correct. Also hypothyroidism, neurosyphilis, depression and NPH.

q.s: Why do people with Down syndrome develop early-onset Alzheimer disease?
o: They have low ACh at birth
The amyloid precursor protein gene is on chromosome 21

q.s: Which ApoE allele increases the risk of sporadic Alzheimer disease?
The number of which lesion correlates with the degree of dementia in Alzheimer disease?
A 55-year-old man has progressive personality change and disinhibition. Biopsy shows round tau inclusions in neurons of the frontal and temporal lobes. Diagnosis?

A 72-year-old man has fluctuating attention, sees children in his room that are not there, acts out dreams and has mild rigidity. Cognitive and motor symptoms began within 6 months of each other. Diagnosis?
A patient with hypertension has stepwise cognitive decline. MRI shows multiple cortical and subcortical infarcts. Diagnosis?
A 60-year-old has rapidly progressive dementia over 3 months with startle myoclonus. EEG shows periodic sharp waves and CSF 14-3-3 protein is elevated. What is the cause?
o: Prions converting PrPc to protease-resistant PrPsc

rounds.t: Intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, multiple sclerosis, and demyelination

q.s: An obese 25-year-old woman has daily headaches and transient visual blurring. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema. MRI is normal except for an empty sella. LP shows high opening pressure with normal CSF. Diagnosis?
Months after bacterial meningitis, a child develops enlarging ventricles with all ventricles dilated. Mechanism?
o: Decreased CSF absorption from arachnoid scarring

q.s: A 74-year-old man has a magnetic, wide-based gait, forgetfulness and urinary incontinence. CT shows enlarged ventricles without increased sulcal size. What is the treatment?
o: CSF drainage via LP or shunt
e: Correct. Normal pressure hydrocephalus ("wobbly, wacky, wet").

q.s: Why does normal pressure hydrocephalus cause gait and bladder symptoms?
o: Ventricular expansion distorts fibers of the corona radiata

q.s: A colloid cyst blocking the foramen of Monro causes:
o: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus with upstream lateral ventricle dilation
Dilation of the fourth ventricle only

q.s: A patient with Alzheimer disease has enlarged ventricles on CT with normal ICP and no NPH triad. This is:

A 28-year-old woman has painful loss of vision in her right eye. A year earlier she had numbness in her legs that resolved. When she bends her neck forward, an electric sensation runs down her spine. What finding is expected in the CSF?
A patient with MS notices that her vision worsens after a hot shower. This is called:
Which MRI finding is typical of multiple sclerosis?
o: Periventricular white matter plaques disseminated in space and time

q.s: Which drug treats acute MS flares?
A patient with MS on natalizumab develops progressive visual loss and confusion. MRI shows nonenhancing parieto-occipital white matter lesions. Which virus is responsible?
An alcoholic patient with a sodium of 108 mEq/L is corrected to 128 mEq/L within 24 hours. Two days later he becomes quadriplegic with dysarthria. Diagnosis?
e: Wrong. From correcting high to low.
Correct. "From low to high, your pons will die."

q.s: Two weeks after diarrhea from undercooked chicken, a man develops ascending leg weakness, absent reflexes and bilateral facial weakness. CSF protein is high with normal cell count. What is the treatment?
o: Plasma exchange or IVIG, with respiratory support

q.s: A 20-year-old has high-arched feet, hammer toes, foot drop and decreased vibration sense. His mother has similar findings. Which genetic change is most common?
A septic patient in the ICU for 3 weeks cannot be weaned from the ventilator. He has symmetric distal weakness and decreased reflexes. Mechanism?
o: Axonal degeneration from inflammatory mediators and Na+ channel inactivation

q.s: MS is more prevalent in which population?
o: Women aged 20–40 in regions farther from the equator

q.s: Which treatment is used for MS-related spasticity?
Correcting hypernatremia too quickly causes:
e: Correct. "From high to low, your brains will blow."

q.s: Which demyelinating disorder is postinfectious?
Which drug treats MS-related urge incontinence?

rounds.t: Neurocutaneous disorders and adult brain tumors

q.s: An infant has a port-wine stain over the V1 distribution, seizures and early glaucoma. Imaging shows ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas with calcifications. Which gene is mutated?
A child with seizures and intellectual disability has hypopigmented ash-leaf spots, facial angiofibromas and a cardiac rhabdomyoma. Which tumor of the kidney is associated?
Tuberous sclerosis increases the incidence of which brain tumor?
A child has more than six café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas and pigmented iris hamartomas. On which chromosome is the mutated gene?
e: Correct. NF1 ("17 letters in von Recklinghausen").

q.s: Neurofibromin, the NF1 gene product, normally:
A 25-year-old has bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI shows bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Which other tumors are associated?
A man has cerebellar hemangioblastoma, retinal angiomas, bilateral renal cell carcinomas and a pheochromocytoma. What does the deleted gene's product normally do?
A 60-year-old man has headaches and personality change. MRI shows a mass crossing the corpus callosum. Biopsy shows pseudopalisading cells around necrosis. Which marker is positive?
Glioblastoma is associated with amplification of which gene?
A slow-growing calcified frontal lobe tumor shows round nuclei with clear cytoplasm and a "chicken-wire" capillary pattern. Diagnosis?
A 50-year-old woman has a well-circumscribed extra-axial mass with a dural tail. Biopsy shows whorled spindle cells and laminated calcifications. Which cell is the origin?
A cerebellar tumor of thin-walled capillaries causes polycythemia. Why?
A 30-year-old woman has amenorrhea, galactorrhea and bitemporal hemianopia. Which cell type is the most common origin of this tumor?
First-line medical treatment for a prolactinoma is:
o: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine

q.s: A 55-year-old has progressive right hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. MRI shows a mass at the right cerebellopontine angle. Biopsy shows alternating dense spindle-cell areas and loose myxoid areas. Diagnosis?
Sudden severe headache, visual loss and hypotension in a patient with a pituitary adenoma suggest:
e: Correct. Hemorrhage into the adenoma causing hypopituitarism.

q.s: The mnemonic "CICLOPSS" describes features of:
e: Correct. Café-au-lait, Intellectual disability, Cutaneous neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, Optic gliomas, Pheochromocytoma, Seizures, bone lesions.

q.s: Tuberous sclerosis genes TSC1 and TSC2 encode:
Which neurocutaneous disorder is NOT inherited?
Most adult primary brain tumors are found in which location?

rounds.t: Childhood brain tumors, herniation, and spinal cord lesions

q.s: An 8-year-old has headaches and unsteadiness. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with a mural nodule. Biopsy shows hairlike projections and Rosenthal fibers. Prognosis?

A 6-year-old has morning vomiting, truncal ataxia and papilledema. MRI shows a vermis mass compressing the fourth ventricle. Biopsy shows small blue cells around neuropil. What is a feared complication?
o: Drop metastases to the spinal cord

q.s: A child has a fourth ventricle tumor causing hydrocephalus. Biopsy shows perivascular pseudorosettes and rod-shaped blepharoplasts. Diagnosis?
A 10-year-old has headaches and bitemporal hemianopia. CT shows a calcified suprasellar mass. Aspiration yields "motor oil" fluid with cholesterol crystals. Diagnosis?
e: Wrong. Not calcified, not in children typically.

q.s: A pineal gland tumor causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus by compressing the:
A patient with a right-sided mass has a dilated right pupil and left hemiparesis. Which herniation is occurring?
Kernohan phenomenon refers to:
o: Contralateral hemiparesis from ipsilateral peduncle compression
Ipsilateral hemiparesis from compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorium

q.s: Cingulate herniation under the falx can compress which artery?
Duret hemorrhages result from:
o: Central transtentorial herniation tearing paramedian basilar branches

q.s: Which sign indicates a lower motor neuron lesion?
o: Fasciculations and atrophy with decreased reflexes

q.s: An unvaccinated child develops fever, neck stiffness and asymmetric flaccid weakness of one leg. CSF shows lymphocytes with normal glucose. Which cells are destroyed?
A 3-month-old is profoundly floppy with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes but alert eyes. Which gene is mutated?
A 58-year-old has weakness with atrophy and fasciculations in his hands, plus spasticity and hyperreflexia in his legs. Sensation and bladder function are normal. Which drug may slow progression?
Familial ALS may be linked to mutations in:
A patient with tertiary syphilis has a wide-based gait that worsens when he closes his eyes, shooting leg pains and absent reflexes. Which pupils are expected?
Subacute combined degeneration affects which tracts?
o: Spinocerebellar, lateral corticospinal and dorsal columns

q.s: After thoracic aortic aneurysm repair, a patient has flaccid leg paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below T10, with preserved vibration and proprioception. Which artery's territory is infarcted?
e: Correct. Artery of Adamkiewicz supplies below T8.

q.s: Clasp-knife spasticity is a sign of:
Which tumor is the most common primary brain tumor in childhood?
Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum is dangerous because it:
o: Compresses the medulla, causing cardiorespiratory arrest

rounds.t: Brown-Séquard, Friedreich ataxia, cerebral palsy, and cranial nerve lesions

q.s: A man stabbed in the back has right leg weakness with hyperreflexia, loss of vibration and proprioception in the right leg, and loss of pain and temperature in the left leg. Where is the lesion?
o: Right hemisection of the spinal cord

q.s: In Brown-Séquard syndrome, a lesion above T1 may also cause:
At the level of a Brown-Séquard lesion, the patient has:
o: Ipsilateral loss of all sensation and LMN signs

q.s: A 12-year-old has progressive staggering gait, frequent falls, scoliosis, high arches and absent reflexes. Echocardiography shows a thick left ventricle. What is the inheritance and repeat?
o: Autosomal recessive GAA repeat in frataxin

q.s: What is the most common cause of death in Friedreich ataxia?
e: Wrong. Associated, but not the cause of death.

q.s: Frataxin is an iron-binding protein whose loss impairs:
A 2-year-old born at 28 weeks has stiff legs, hyperreflexia and delayed walking. MRI shows periventricular leukomalacia. Diagnosis?
Which prenatal intervention reduces the incidence of cerebral palsy in high-risk pregnancies?
A patient's jaw deviates to the left when he opens his mouth. Which nerve is injured?
e: Correct. Unopposed right pterygoid pushes the jaw toward the lesion.

q.s: A patient's uvula deviates to the right when he says "ah." Which nerve is injured?
e: Wrong. Uvula points away from the lesion.

q.s: After a neck dissection, a patient's right shoulder droops and he has difficulty turning his head to the left. Which nerve is injured?
A patient's tongue deviates to the right on protrusion, with right-sided tongue atrophy and fasciculations. Where is the lesion?
e: Wrong. Would deviate right but without atrophy.

q.s: A 35-year-old woman wakes with inability to close her right eye, a drooping right mouth corner and inability to wrinkle her right forehead. She has hyperacusis on the right. What is the treatment?
e: Wrong. Stroke would spare the forehead.

q.s: A stroke patient has weakness of the lower left face, but can wrinkle his forehead on both sides. Why is the forehead spared?
o: The forehead is supplied by CN V
The forehead has no motor supply
The lesion is in the facial nucleus
The upper face has bilateral UMN innervation

q.s: A man has right facial paralysis, ear pain and vesicles in his right ear canal. Which virus is responsible?
Which is a cause of bilateral peripheral facial palsy?
Which symptom accompanies an LMN facial nerve lesion but not a UMN lesion?
o: Incomplete eye closure, hyperacusis and loss of taste on the anterior tongue

q.s: An UMN lesion of CN XII causes the tongue to deviate:
o: Toward the side of the lesion
Away from the side of the lesion

q.s: Cerebral palsy presents with which motor signs?
o: Progressive weakness and death in infancy
UMN signs such as spasticity and hyperreflexia, with persistence of primitive reflexes

q.s: A complete Brown-Séquard lesion causes contralateral loss of which sensation below the lesion?
o: Pain and temperature, starting 1–2 segments below
e: Correct. Spinothalamic tract crosses at the anterior white commissure.
